source: Hollan, Hutchins, Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Distributed cognition (DC) defines a cognitive process by the functional relations among its elements, not by where they sit (skull or skin). The unit of analysis can be a ship bridge or an airline cockpit.
numbers: No numbers. Three kinds of distribution named: across people, between internal and external structure, and through time.
limits: Programmatic paper for HCI, not an experiment. Its claims rest on Hutchins' field studies.
agent_relevance: Treat the agent plus its tools, files, checks and code as one system. Judge the system, not the model alone. Fits the schema design view (program decides, model fills slots).

source: Hollan, Hutchins, Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: Three distributions of process: (1) across members of a social group, (2) coordination of internal and external structure, (3) through time so earlier products change later events. Social organisation is itself a form of cognitive architecture because it fixes how information flows.
numbers: Three questions for groups: how individual-mind processes are implemented in a group; how group properties differ from members; how membership changes individual minds.
limits: Time-distribution (3) has the thinnest evidence in the paper.
agent_relevance: Map to agent design: (1) multi-agent roles, (2) tool and scratchpad use, (3) persistent artefacts across runs. A checklist for what our schema distributes.

source: Hollan, Hutchins, Kirsh (2000) Distributed cognition: toward a new foundation for HCI research
finding: DC says cognition is embodied and causally coupled to the environment. Culture is a history of artefacts and practices that shapes cognition of systems larger than one person. Work materials can become elements of the cognitive system.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Conceptual. Ties to Suchman (plans and situated action) and Hutchins' book. No quantitative support given.
agent_relevance: Artefacts that persist (notes, test results, shared memory) are part of the thinking system. Supports durable external state with defined formats.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Hutchins applies standard cognitive-science questions (how are representations transformed and propagated) to a unit larger than a person: the airliner cockpit. He states such systems have cognitive properties that cannot be reduced to those of the individual persons.
numbers: Ethnographic base: more than 100 flights observed as observer crew member; about 6 years of aviation safety research (author's own count).
quote: systems that are larger than an individual may have cognitive properties in their own right that cannot be reduced to the cognitive properties of individual persons
limits: One analyst, one aircraft type (MD-80), a stylised account, no controlled comparison. Hutchins says he leaves out extended raw observations.
agent_relevance: Founding claim of the field. Also the template for analysing an agent loop as a representational system: what is written, in what medium, who reads it.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Case: landing speeds. Pilots look up gross weight, post the matching speed card (weight filters the booklet), set speed bugs on the airspeed dial, and cross-check with the other pilot. Memory for speeds lives in the card booklet, bug positions, spoken callouts and pilot memory together.
numbers: Example card speeds: 227 knots minimum maneuvering speed with no flaps; 152 with flaps 15 and slats extended; 128 landing speed at flaps 40. Final-approach callouts when airspeed varies by more than 5 knots.
quote: Speed bugs do not help pilots remember speeds; rather, they are part of the process by which the cockpit system remembers speeds.
limits: Numbers are from one airline procedure for one aircraft type. Not a statistical study.
agent_relevance: Offload a computation into a representation that turns it into a perceptual match (bug on dial), and cross-check with a second independent representation. Our held-out checks (G3) play the bug role.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Three redundant representations of the same speeds: card, spoken words, bug positions. Redundancy lets the crew detect a wrong weight, because the card shows its weight and the fuel panel shows gross weight a few inches away.
numbers: Transposition errors named as the most frequent reading error (cited to Norman 1991 and Wickens & Flach 1988; not measured here).
quote: The cockpit system remembers its speeds, and the memory process emerges from the activity of the pilots.
limits: The error-rate claim is secondhand and probable, not measured in this paper.
agent_relevance: Redundant, differently-formed records plus a cheap cross-check catch a class of errors. Suggests holding a plan in two forms (text plus checkable code) and comparing them.

source: Hutchins (1995) How a cockpit remembers its speeds
finding: Properties of memory in a system with external media depend on the medium: how long the representation lasts, which sense reads it, how vulnerable it is. Individual-memory theory explains why the system needs so many external parts, not how the system works.
numbers: No numbers.
quote: The memory of the cockpit, however, is not made primarily of pilot memory.
limits: Argument by analysis, not experiment.
agent_relevance: Choose where the agent stores state by the property needed: durability, checkability, cost to re-read. Persisting only in the context window loses endurance.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Framework of distributed representations: a task has internal and external representations, and the same abstract rules can sit in memory or in the physical display. Four rules of Tower of Hanoi isomorphs were made internal (stated and memorised) or external (built into objects such as cup sizes and stacking constraints).
numbers: Experiments: 1A N=24 undergraduates; 1B N=24; 2 N=18; 3 N=36. Four levels of isomorphism: rule distribution, problem-space structure, rule representation, dimension representation. Rules memorised for 2 minutes then recited before play.
limits: Fixed start and end positions (authors cite limited subject numbers). Small student samples. Solution time, steps and errors used as difficulty.
agent_relevance: Core evidence that the same logical task changes in difficulty with where the rules live. Supports moving rules from the prompt into code constraints.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Experiment 2: the more rules were external, the easier the problem, with fewer errors, steps and time. No errors at all were made on external rules; all errors were on internal rules.
numbers: N=18; conditions II23 (all internal), II2-E3, II-E23. Main effect p<.05 for time and steps, p<.005 for errors. II23 vs II-E23 errors p<.001. II2-E3 vs II-E23 not significant.
quote: external rules seem to be error proof
limits: Small N. Authors note external rules were perceptually available or physically constrained, so perception and constraint are mixed.
agent_relevance: Supports code-enforced constraints: a rule the environment enforces cannot be violated, a rule the model must remember can. A prediction to test with hard legality checks.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Experiments 1A (all rules internal) and 1B (all but one external) gave different difficulty orders. With all rules internal, the middle-constraint problem (II23) was hardest. With external rules, difficulty rose with the number of rules. No errors in 1B.
numbers: 1A N=24: difficulty II < II3 < II234 ~ II23 (times and errors). 1B N=24: II < II-E3 <= II-E23 <= II-E234. Solution times of easiest vs hardest problem differ by as much as 1 to 10. Scores divided by minimum steps (2, 4, 7, 8).
limits: The link to working-memory load is a post hoc explanation, not tested directly.
agent_relevance: A more constrained problem is not automatically easier: it depends on where constraints are held.

source: Zhang & Norman (1994) Representations in distributed cognitive tasks
finding: Experiment 3: the same ordinal or nominal dimension shown by location beat size and colour on most measures.
numbers: N=36. Ordinal: size vs location times p<.01, errors p<.03. Nominal: size vs location times p<.003, errors p<.0001; location vs colour times p<.016, errors p<.007. Step differences mostly not significant. Colour vs size not significant.
limits: Authors say the colour ordering was trivial to memorise, which may hide a difference. Steps rarely significant.
agent_relevance: Format of the same information matters. A spatial or tabular layout may beat prose for ordering and comparison. Test it for the agent, do not assume.

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Epistemic actions are physical actions that make mental computation easier, faster or more reliable. In Tetris, players rotate and translate pieces more than needed to place them, and the extra moves fit best as using the world to think, not as false starts.
numbers: Rotation begins by 400 to 600 ms, sometimes under 100 ms. A plan-then-act account predicts about 1.5 rotations for a four-orientation piece; data (Fig 6) show more. Average interval between keystrokes about 250 ms, minimum about 75 ms.
limits: Tetris only, few players, argument from data patterns, no controlled intervention.
agent_relevance: Names a kind of useful extra step. A draft, test run or reformat is an epistemic action: it changes the problem so the next judgement is easier. Compare with G1 (doubt only on a signal).

source: Kirsh & Maglio (1994) On distinguishing epistemic from pragmatic action
finding: Pilot mental rotation task shows physical rotation is far cheaper than mental rotation for Tetris pieces.
numbers: Physical 90 degree rotation in as few as 100 ms vs about 800 to 1200 ms mental (estimate from pilot). Three players (intermediate, advanced, expert), eight presentations of each pair type; reaction time rose with angular difference 0 to 180 degrees.
limits: N=3 pilot, Shepard-Metzler style task. Authors note priming may shrink the gap but still expect a large difference.
agent_relevance: Order-of-magnitude saving from acting on the world instead of simulating it. LLM analogue: run code instead of mental arithmetic.

source: Hutchins (1995) Cognition in the Wild (not read; known through HHK 2000 and the cockpit paper)
finding: Founding study: ethnography of navigation on a Navy ship. Navigation is a computation done by a team plus instruments, charts and routines, and the team's cognition differs from any member's. Culture and the history of artefacts shape the task.
numbers: Not read. SEP says the load of navigating a large Navy vessel exceeds the capacity of any single individual.
limits: Book not opened; second-hand descriptions only. Ethnography, no controls.
agent_relevance: Origin story only. Use the cockpit paper for evidence.

source: Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, Embodied Cognition, section 2.2
finding: SEP uses Hutchins only as an example of embedded cognition: the load of navigating a large Navy vessel is spread across specialists.
numbers: No numbers. The term distributed cognition did not appear in the part read (first 100000 of 114500 characters).
quote: The cognitive load required to navigate a large Navy vessel exceeds the capacity of any single individual
limits: Philosophy overview; page partly read.
agent_relevance: Philosophy treats this as embedded, not extended, cognition. Do not overclaim.

source: Wegner, Erber, Raymond (1991) Transactive memory in close relationships (as described by Harris et al. 2011)
finding: Close couples recalled more than stranger pairs only when they used their own division of memory responsibility. When the experimenter assigned categories, strangers recalled more than couples.
numbers: Sample 118 individuals in dating relationships of at least 3 months (from a search snippet). Categorised word-list recall. Effect sizes not recorded.
limits: Original PDF not obtained (access denied); known only through Harris et al.
agent_relevance: Imposed role splits can break a working informal division of labour. For multi-agent roles, fixed persona splits may do worse than letting competence decide who answers (supports G4: no persona voters).

source: Harris, Keil, Sutton, Barnier, McIlwain (2011) We remember, we forget: collaborative remembering in older couples
finding: Older long-married couples sometimes show collaborative inhibition (worse as a pair) and sometimes collaborative facilitation. Group-level strategy use predicted who benefited.
numbers: 12 couples (24 people), ages 60 to 89, married 26 to 60 years (mean 40.67 years). Word list: on the first test couples recalled 9.50 words (SD 1.08) as a nominal group and 8.92 (SD 2.11) as a collaborative group.
quote: Across each of the tasks, although some couples demonstrated collaborative inhibition, others demonstrated collaborative facilitation.
limits: N=12 couples recruited from Rotary clubs, mixed qualitative method. Not a strict replication of Wegner 1991.
agent_relevance: Pooling is not automatically better. Gains depend on the group's strategy, which has to be organised, not just added.

source: Fansher, Shah, Helie (undated preprint, about 2020) The effect of mode of presentation on Tower of Hanoi problem solving
finding: A modern test in the Zhang & Norman line. External (computer) presentation raised completion, but mental presentation gave solutions in fewer moves; people paused longer between moves when solving mentally.
numbers: Experiment 1: completion 100% computer vs 91% mental, chi-square(1)=4.45, p=.03; progress 4.00 vs 3.61, t(35)=2.44, p=.02; N=135 after exclusions; at least 30 per condition chosen by convenience. Experiment 2 on Prolific workers.
limits: Preprint; year is approximate. Not the same manipulation as Z&N (mode of presentation, not rule location). Authors suggest external supports speed, internal supports planning.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: external support raises success but may lower strategy quality (more moves). Tool-using agents may finish while skipping planning. Track move count, not only solve rate.

source: Du, Li, Torralba, Tenenbaum, Mordatch (2023) Improving factuality and reasoning in language models through multiagent debate
finding: Several ChatGPT instances answer, read each other's answers and revise. Debate beat a single agent, reflection and majority vote on every task tried.
numbers: 3 agents, 2 rounds. Arithmetic: single 67.0, reflection 72.1, majority 69.0, debate 81.8. GSM8K: 77.0, 75.0, 81.0, 85.0. Chess pawn score: 91.4, 102.1, 102.2, 122.9. Biographies: single 66.0, reflection 68.3, debate 73.8. MMLU: 63.9, 57.7, debate 71.1 (74.2 with different personas). Chess move validity: 29.3, 38.8, 45.2.
limits: One model family (ChatGPT, 2023). Cost grows with agents and rounds. Later work finds the gain does not hold against stronger baselines.
agent_relevance: The strongest early pro-collective result. Contrast with later controls. Debate is not independent voting; G4 says agreement is not proof.

source: Li, Zhang, Yu, Fu, Ye (2024) More agents is all you need
finding: Plain sampling and voting (Agent Forest) with more instances raises accuracy, more so on harder tasks. A smaller model with enough samples can match a larger one.
numbers: Gains from larger ensembles: GSM8K 12 to 24 points, MATH 6 to 10, Chess 1 to 4, MMLU 5 to 11, HumanEval 4 to 9. Llama2-13B reached 59% on GSM8K vs Llama2-70B 54%.
limits: Samples from one model are correlated, so returns diminish.
agent_relevance: The cheap form of distribution: independent samples plus a code-side vote. Fits G5 (code selects), unlike debate.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) Stop overvaluing multi-agent debate
finding: A systematic test of 5 multi-agent debate methods on 9 benchmarks with 4 models finds debate often fails to beat chain-of-thought or self-consistency, even with more compute. Model heterogeneity helps.
numbers: No debate method wins more than 20% of 36 scenarios (4 models x 9 benchmarks) against CoT. Underperformance is larger against self-consistency at matched calls or tokens.
limits: Position paper plus benchmark study; methods not tuned for heterogeneity.
agent_relevance: Failed-replication style evidence against Du et al. 2023. Supports not adding a debate stage by default (section 4b).

source: Smit, Grinsztajn, Duckworth, Barrett, Pretorius (2024) Should we be going MAD?
finding: Comparison of multi-agent debate strategies finds they do not consistently outperform other ensembling strategies and are sensitive to hyperparameters.
numbers: Exact figures not extracted; conclusions read from the text only.
limits: Skimmed by keyword search; no numbers recorded.
agent_relevance: Second independent source for the negative result on debate.

source: Cemri et al. (2025) Why do multi-agent LLM systems fail?
finding: MAST taxonomy: 14 failure modes in 3 clusters, built from 150 traces and applied to 1600+ traces across 7 frameworks. Failure rates 41% to 86.7% across frameworks.
numbers: Human annotator kappa 0.88; LLM judge kappa 0.77. Clusters: system design 41.8%, inter-agent misalignment 36.9%, task verification 21.3%. Better role specification gave +9.4% on ChatDev; adding a verification step gave +15.6% on ProgramDev.
quote: Successful systems all work alike; each failing system has its own problems.
limits: Open-source frameworks; GPT-4o interventions; counts depend on an LLM judge.
agent_relevance: The distributed system fails at the joints human teams do: specification, hand-offs, verification. Supports code-side verification and fixed hand-off formats.

source: Kim et al. (2025/2026) Towards a science of scaling agent systems
finding: Controlled study of 260 configurations: 6 benchmarks, 5 architectures (single plus 4 multi-agent), 3 model families. Coordination helps on decomposable tasks and hurts on sequential or tool-heavy ones. A single-agent baseline above about 45% leaves little room for gains.
numbers: Range from +80.8% (Finance Agent, centralized) to -70.0% (PlanCraft, independent). Capability ceiling beta=-0.236, p=0.004. Independent agents amplify errors 17.2x, centralized 4.4x. Predicts the best architecture for 87% of held-out configurations. Cross-validated R2=0.373.
limits: Own taxonomy; 87% is on held-out configurations of the same study. The 45% threshold is empirical, not a law.
agent_relevance: Best controlled evidence on when distribution helps. Split work only when subtasks are separable, and add a central verifier if you add agents.

source: Shang et al. (2026) United minds or isolated agents? (CoThinker)
finding: Multi-agent design built on cognitive-load theory with a transactive-memory component. Gains on reasoning-heavy tasks; coordination overhead dominates on instruction-following.
numbers: Examples: Data Analysis +16.2% vs IO (p<.001); Reasoning +15.5% vs CoT (p=0.001); Language +18.3% vs SR (p<.001). Transactive-memory component was less effective on newer GPT models that refuse to expose step-by-step reasoning.
limits: Gains vary by comparator and benchmark; some comparisons not significant (p=0.63, 0.17). Gemini is the main backbone.
agent_relevance: Boundary condition: distribution helps above a load threshold only, which matches the Kim et al. ceiling. Shared state needs visible reasoning.

source: Kim et al. (2026) Multi-Agent Transactive Memory (MATM)
finding: A shared repository of agent trajectories that other agents retrieve is a machine version of transactive memory. Retrieval raised success without joint training.
numbers: ALFWorld success 47% to 55% (+8.0 points), steps per episode 11.77 to 11.18. WebArena 18% to 20%. Tokens per successful episode down 11 to 34% for single consumer agents. WebArena with reranker 64.3%-type figure appears in another setting (+9.2 over single-stage); check table before quoting.
limits: WebArena gain is small (2 points); a dip at intermediate corpus size; trajectories from mixed models.
agent_relevance: Cross-run external memory of what worked is distribution through time (HHK type 3). Needs reranking and selective retrieval.

source: Wu et al. (2026) Scaling teams or scaling time? LLMA-Mem
finding: Lifelong memory for multi-agent systems on MultiAgentBench shows non-monotonic scaling: larger teams are not always better, and smaller teams with good memory can beat larger ones.
numbers: Exact numbers not recorded (abstract and scaling statements only).
limits: Only the abstract and scaling statements were checked.
agent_relevance: Spend on memory reuse before spending on more agents.
